title: Genital Mycoplasmas: M. genitalium Macrolide Resistance and the hominis–Ureaplasma Drug Swap
summary: Learn why wall-less genital mycoplasmas ignore β-lactams, how 23S rRNA mutations make Mycoplasma genitalium macrolide-resistant, the CDC 2021 two-stage regimen, and why Mycoplasma hominis resists erythromycin and azithromycin while Ureaplasma resists clindamycin.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 62 Hit 4 (M. genitalium in NGNC urethritis; M. hominis macrolide resistance; Ureaplasma clindamycin resistance), Hit 5 (M. genitalium macrolide resistance, 23S rRNA 2058/2059, moxifloxacin) and Trap 2 (the hominis–Ureaplasma drug swap). Checked against Workowski 2021 (CDC STI guidelines, full text via Europe PMC), Getman 2016, Redelinghuys 2014, Xiang 2019 and Waites 2025. Qualifications: Hit 4 calls M. genitalium the most common cause of NGNC urethritis, which the sources read do not state (CDC 2021: 20–25% of nonchlamydial NGU, no pathogen in about half of NGU; proposed flag rv-ch62-mg-ngnc-most-common); Hit 5 gives moxifloxacin for 7–10 days after azithromycin failure, while CDC 2021 uses two-stage therapy, doxycycline then moxifloxacin for 7 days, and says a 1-g azithromycin dose should not be used (proposed flag rv-ch62-mg-moxifloxacin-two-stage); the 42–51% US figure comes from one 2013–2014 cohort (Getman 2016), and CDC gives 44–90% across four regions (proposed flag rv-ch62-mg-macrolide-resistance-range). Not taught: M. hominis tetracycline resistance (Number Vault), the 10–35% NGNC figure in 5-Second Recall. US regimens; Philippine guidance is not covered.

objectives: Explain why β-lactams and vancomycin do not act on genital mycoplasmas and why M. genitalium is diagnosed by NAAT rather than culture.
Describe 23S rRNA 2058/2059 macrolide resistance in M. genitalium and the CDC 2021 two-stage, resistance-guided regimen.
Match M. hominis and Ureaplasma to the drug class each is naturally resistant to and to the classes that remain active.

scenes.title: Three mycoplasma reports, three drug plans
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three reports reach the clinic. (1) A man with urethritis that came back after treatment; urine NAAT positive for Mycoplasma genitalium; plan: azithromycin 1 g once. (2) Mycoplasma hominis grown from a genital specimen; plan: azithromycin. (3) Ureaplasma grown from a genital specimen; plan: clindamycin. Question token: “Which plans should be changed?”

cues.text: Three reports reach the clinic. A man whose urethritis came back has a urine NAAT positive for Mycoplasma genitalium. The plan: one gram of azithromycin, once.
A genital culture grows Mycoplasma hominis, and the plan is azithromycin. Another grows Ureaplasma, and the plan is clindamycin.
Three organisms without a cell wall, three drug plans. Which plans should be changed?

scenes.title: Meet the genital mycoplasmas
scenes.altText: Schematic: a wall-less mycoplasma cell. Card “No cell wall”: β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins) and glycopeptides such as vancomycin do not work. Card “M. genitalium” (CDC 2021): causes urethritis in men; about 15–25% of NGU in the United States, 20–25% of nonchlamydial NGU and about 40% of persistent or recurrent urethritis; even with extensive testing, no pathogen is found in about half of NGU. Card “Lab”: culture can take up to 6 months and is a research tool; FDA-cleared NAAT for urine and urethral, penile meatal, endocervical and vaginal swabs. Card “M. hominis and Ureaplasma”: data are inconsistent on their role in urethritis, most men with Ureaplasma have no overt disease unless the organism load is high, and CDC does not recommend testing for them in cervicitis.

cues.text: Mycoplasmas have no cell wall. So drugs that attack the wall, penicillins, cephalosporins and vancomycin, simply do not work on them.

Mycoplasma genitalium causes urethritis in men. CDC puts it at about fifteen to twenty-five percent of nongonococcal urethritis in the United States, twenty to twenty-five percent of the nonchlamydial cases, and about forty percent of urethritis that persists or returns.
It grows so slowly that culture can take up to six months, so the lab uses an FDA-cleared NAAT on urine or on urethral, penile, cervical or vaginal swabs.
Mycoplasma hominis and Ureaplasma are different. Their role in urethritis is inconsistent, and CDC does not recommend testing for them in women with cervicitis.

scenes.title: How M. genitalium escapes azithromycin
scenes.altText: Schematic: the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit with a mutation at position 2058 or 2059 (E. coli numbering, region V); 23S rRNA changes can interfere with macrolide binding to the 50S ribosome. Card “US cohort” (Getman 2016, specimens collected 2013–2014 at seven US sites): 2058/2059 mutations in 50.8% (65/128) of M. genitalium-infected women and 42% (21/50) of infected men whose specimens were sequenced. Card “CDC 2021”: macrolide-resistance markers in 44–90% across the United States, Canada, Western Europe and Australia; markers correlate highly with treatment failure; a 1-g azithromycin dose selects resistant populations in 10–12% of macrolide-susceptible infections. Token: quinolone-resistance markers much rarer; parC S83I linked to the first moxifloxacin failures.

cues.text: Macrolides bind the 50S ribosome, and changes in its 23S RNA can block that binding. In Mycoplasma genitalium, mutations at position 2058 or 2059 of the 23S RNA are known to give high-level macrolide resistance.

In one multicentre United States cohort, with specimens collected in 2013 and 2014, these mutations were found in about fifty-one percent of infected women and forty-two percent of infected men whose strains were sequenced.

CDC’s 2021 guideline gives forty-four to ninety percent across the United States, Canada, Western Europe and Australia. The markers track closely with treatment failure, and a single one-gram azithromycin dose selects resistance in ten to twelve percent of susceptible infections.
Quinolone-resistance markers are much less common, although a parC mutation, S83I, was linked to the first moxifloxacin failures.

scenes.title: Matching drug to organism
scenes.altText: Left card: M. genitalium, CDC 2021 two-stage therapy: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days first; then, if macrolide-susceptible, azithromycin 1 g then 500 mg daily for 3 days (2.5 g total); if macrolide-resistant or resistance testing unavailable, moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 7 days; a single 1-g azithromycin dose should not be used; resistance tests were not commercially available in the United States in 2021. Right card: drug-swap table — M. hominis: intrinsically resistant to 14- and 15-membered macrolides (erythromycin, azithromycin); clindamycin, quinolones and tetracyclines are active. Ureaplasma: naturally resistant to lincosamides (clindamycin); macrolides, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones are the main options, with acquired resistance documented. Hook answer token: all three plans should be changed.

cues.text: For Mycoplasma genitalium, CDC uses two stages. Doxycycline for seven days lowers the organism load. Then, if the strain is macrolide-susceptible, high-dose azithromycin, two point five grams over four days. If it is resistant, or no resistance test is available, moxifloxacin four hundred milligrams daily for seven days.
Mycoplasma hominis is intrinsically resistant to erythromycin and azithromycin, but clindamycin, quinolones and tetracyclines are active against it.
Ureaplasma is the mirror image: naturally resistant to clindamycin. Macrolides, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones are its main options, although acquired resistance to each has been documented.

So all three hook plans should be changed. The single azithromycin dose should not be used, Mycoplasma hominis is intrinsically resistant to azithromycin, and Ureaplasma is naturally resistant to clindamycin.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Treat M. hominis with azithromycin” (✓ intrinsically resistant to 14- and 15-membered macrolides; clindamycin, quinolones or tetracyclines are active); “Treat Ureaplasma with clindamycin” (✓ naturally resistant to lincosamides; use a macrolide, tetracycline or fluoroquinolone); “One gram of azithromycin cures M. genitalium” (✓ CDC 2021: do not use a single 1-g dose; two-stage, resistance-guided therapy).

cues.text: Trap one: treat Mycoplasma hominis with azithromycin. No: it is intrinsically resistant to erythromycin and azithromycin. Clindamycin, a quinolone or a tetracycline is active.
Trap two: treat Ureaplasma with clindamycin. No: Ureaplasma is naturally resistant to it. Choose a macrolide, a tetracycline or a fluoroquinolone.
Trap three: a single gram of azithromycin cures Mycoplasma genitalium. No: CDC says that dose should not be used. Doxycycline comes first, then a drug chosen by resistance.

scenes.title: The mirror pair
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The mirror pair: M. Hominis Mocks Macrolides, Ureaplasma Ignores clIndamycin — each one tolerates the drug that treats the other. And genitalium? Doxy first, then the resistance test picks the second drug.” Tokens: hominis ✗ macrolides · Ureaplasma ✗ clindamycin · genitalium: doxy → test. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the mirror pair. Hominis mocks macrolides; Ureaplasma ignores clindamycin. Each tolerates the drug that treats the other. And genitalium: doxycycline first, then the resistance test picks the second drug.

Where it breaks: Ureaplasma can acquire resistance to macrolides, tetracyclines and quinolones; the hominis resistance named here is to erythromycin and azithromycin; resistance tests are not always available; and these are United States regimens.

scenes.altText: Two tokens: “M. genitalium: doxycycline first → moxifloxacin or high-dose azithromycin by resistance; no single 1-g azithromycin”, “M. hominis ✗ erythromycin/azithromycin · Ureaplasma ✗ clindamycin”.

cues.text: Treat Mycoplasma genitalium with doxycycline first and then moxifloxacin or high-dose azithromycin chosen by resistance, and remember that Mycoplasma hominis resists erythromycin and azithromycin while Ureaplasma resists clindamycin.

props.label: M. genitalium: doxy → moxi or high-dose azithro by resistance

explanation.what: Plain language: mycoplasmas are tiny bacteria with no cell wall, so wall-attacking antibiotics do nothing to them. One of them, Mycoplasma genitalium, causes urethritis and has learned to dodge azithromycin, so doctors give doxycycline first and then a second drug, ideally chosen by a resistance test. Two relatives, Mycoplasma hominis and Ureaplasma, each ignore a different drug: hominis ignores erythromycin and azithromycin, Ureaplasma ignores clindamycin. Scientific terms: Mollicutes, nongonococcal urethritis (NGU), nonchlamydial NGU, nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), 23S rRNA, A2058/A2059 (E. coli numbering, domain V), macrolide resistance marker, parC S83I, resistance-guided two-stage therapy, intrinsic (natural) resistance, lincosamides, tet(M).
explanation.why: Without a cell wall there is no target for β-lactams or glycopeptides. Macrolides bind the 50S ribosome, and 23S rRNA changes can interfere with that binding; in M. genitalium, mutations at 2058 or 2059 are known to give high-level resistance, and a 1-g azithromycin dose can select resistant populations. M. hominis is intrinsically resistant to 14- and 15-membered macrolides, while Ureaplasma is naturally resistant to lincosamides, so each is treated with the drug that fails against the other.
explanation.measure: M. genitalium (CDC 2021): ~15–25% of US NGU, 20–25% of nonchlamydial NGU, ~40% of persistent or recurrent urethritis; culture up to 6 months; FDA-cleared NAAT on urine and urethral, penile meatal, endocervical and vaginal swabs; test men with recurrent NGU and women with recurrent cervicitis, consider in PID, no screening of asymptomatic people. Macrolide-resistance markers 44–90% (US, Canada, Western Europe, Australia); US cohort 2013–2014: 50.8% of infected women, 42% of infected men sequenced. CDC 2021 gives the M. genitalium share of NGU as 15–25% (Urethritis section), 15–20% (M. genitalium section) and 10–25% (NGU section). Regimens: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 7 d, then azithromycin 1 g + 500 mg daily × 3 d (macrolide-susceptible) or moxifloxacin 400 mg daily × 7 d (resistant or testing unavailable). Ureaplasma (North America 2012–2023): erythromycin resistance 0–10%, fluoroquinolone 0–11.1%, tetracycline 0–30.4% by year.
explanation.differs: M. genitalium (established NGU cause, NAAT, macrolide resistance acquired by 23S mutation) vs M. hominis (intrinsic resistance to erythromycin and azithromycin; clindamycin-susceptible) vs Ureaplasma (intrinsic clindamycin resistance; macrolides, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones usable); intrinsic vs acquired resistance.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick the drug that will fail against M. hominis or Ureaplasma, name the 23S rRNA mutation positions behind M. genitalium macrolide resistance, choose the regimen for M. genitalium when resistance testing is unavailable, or explain why β-lactams do not work on mycoplasmas.

comparisons.distinguisher: Each tolerates the drug class that treats the other.

comparisons.title: Intrinsic vs acquired resistance
comparisons.distinguisher: Expected for the species vs selected in some strains.

mnemonic.text: The mirror pair: M. Hominis Mocks Macrolides, Ureaplasma Ignores clIndamycin — each one tolerates the drug that treats the other. And genitalium? Doxy first, then the resistance test picks the second drug.
mnemonic.explanation: Pairs each organism with the drug class it naturally resists and recalls the two-stage M. genitalium regimen.
mnemonic.limitation: Ureaplasma can acquire macrolide, tetracycline and quinolone resistance, and tet(M)-mediated tetracycline resistance is described in genital mycoplasmas; the M. hominis resistance taught is to erythromycin and azithromycin (14- and 15-membered macrolides); resistance tests are not always available; regimens are US (CDC 2021).

analogyLimitations: Ribosome and organism drawings are schematic.
Resistance rates vary by region, year and testing method.
takeaway: Treat Mycoplasma genitalium with doxycycline first and then moxifloxacin or high-dose azithromycin chosen by resistance, and remember that Mycoplasma hominis resists erythromycin and azithromycin while Ureaplasma resists clindamycin.

questions.stem: A Ureaplasma species is isolated from a genital specimen. Which antimicrobial class is it naturally (intrinsically) resistant to?

options.rationale: Correct. Ureaplasma species are naturally resistant to lincosamides.
Incorrect. Tetracyclines are one of the main classes used for Ureaplasma; resistance (tet(M)) is acquired by some strains, not intrinsic.
Incorrect. Macrolides are a main option for Ureaplasma; intrinsic macrolide resistance belongs to M. hominis.
Incorrect. Fluoroquinolones are a main option; resistance occurs through acquired parC/parE or gyrA/gyrB mutations.

questions.stem: A man with recurrent nongonococcal urethritis has a positive FDA-cleared NAAT for Mycoplasma genitalium. No macrolide-resistance test is available. Which regimen does the CDC 2021 guideline recommend?

options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days, then moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Correct. This is the recommended regimen when resistance testing is not available.

options.text: Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose
options.rationale: Incorrect. Because of high macrolide resistance and selection of resistance, a single 1-g azithromycin dose should not be used.
Incorrect. M. genitalium lacks a cell wall, so β-lactams such as cephalosporins are ineffective.
Incorrect. Clindamycin is not part of the CDC M. genitalium regimens; it is an option for M. hominis.

questions.stem: In a US multicentre study, macrolide resistance markers in Mycoplasma genitalium were identified by sequencing the 23S rRNA. Which change was the marker?

options.text: Mutations at positions 2058/2059 of the 23S rRNA
options.rationale: Correct. These region V mutations (E. coli numbering) confer high-level macrolide resistance and were found in 50.8% of infected women and 42% of infected men whose specimens were sequenced.
Incorrect. parC S83I is associated with moxifloxacin (quinolone) treatment failure, not macrolide resistance.
Incorrect. tet(M) is the known mechanism of tetracycline resistance in Ureaplasma.
Incorrect. The absence of a cell wall explains β-lactam inactivity in genital mycoplasmas; it is not a macrolide-resistance marker.

claims.text: No cell wall: β-lactams and glycopeptides ineffective against genital mycoplasmas.
M. genitalium share of NGU, nonchlamydial NGU and persistent/recurrent urethritis; no pathogen in about half of NGU; other Mycoplasma/Ureaplasma inconsistent; no testing for them in cervicitis.
Culture up to 6 months; FDA-cleared NAAT specimen types; who to test; resistance tests not commercially available in the US (2021).

23S rRNA 2058/2059 mutations; US cohort 50.8% of infected women, 42% of infected men sequenced; 23S changes interfere with macrolide binding; CDC 44–90%; correlation with failure; 1-g azithromycin selection 10–12%; quinolone markers rarer, parC S83I.
CDC 2021 two-stage regimens; single 1-g azithromycin should not be used.

M. hominis intrinsically resistant to erythromycin/azithromycin, clindamycin/quinolones/tetracyclines active; Ureaplasma naturally resistant to lincosamides, macrolides/tetracyclines/fluoroquinolones the main options with acquired resistance documented.
M. genitalium as “the most common” cause of NGNC urethritis; moxifloxacin for 7–10 days; 10–35% of NGNC cases; M. hominis tetracycline resistance ~40%.

claims.text: Scenario invented; ribosome and organism drawings schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 62 Hit 4 calls M. genitalium the most common cause of nongonococcal nonchlamydial urethritis. CDC 2021 gives 20–25% of nonchlamydial NGU and about 40% of persistent or recurrent urethritis (and T. vaginalis 1–8% of NGU), and notes no pathogen is identified in about half of NGU; it does not explicitly rank M. genitalium as the most common cause. The lesson teaches the CDC figures (proposed register flag rv-ch62-mg-ngnc-most-common).

Ch. 62 Hit 5 gives moxifloxacin 400 mg for 7–10 days after azithromycin failure. CDC 2021 recommends two-stage, resistance-guided therapy: doxycycline for 7 days, then high-dose azithromycin (macrolide-susceptible) or moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 7 days (resistant or testing unavailable), and says a single 1-g azithromycin dose should not be used. US guidance; Philippine guidance is not covered (proposed register flag rv-ch62-mg-moxifloxacin-two-stage).

Ch. 62 Hit 5 gives US macrolide resistance in M. genitalium as ~42–51%. This matches one manufacturer-funded multicentre cohort with specimens from 2013–2014 (Getman 2016: 42% of infected men and 50.8% of infected women whose specimens were sequenced); CDC 2021 gives 44–90% across the US, Canada, Western Europe and Australia. The lesson teaches both with dates (proposed register flag rv-ch62-mg-macrolide-resistance-range).
